title: a second bus exits quietly while the first holds bus.lock, and --force replaces it
intention: A bus started while the first holds bus.lock exits 0 with nothing on stdout or stderr and leaves the first serving; --force kills the old bus and takes the claim; the bus.lock path carries the cairn instance.
why: Measured 2026-11-13: the bus loser exits EXIT_HELD=3 with a stderr line (bus/server.py:965-967), but outline 5.3.5.2 says a second copy exits quietly, and Akien said (5.3.5.2.2, said in akiendell's session) a second ground loop 'should see the first, and that it's fine, and exit quietly' and '--force, which means kill the old one'. The bus extension is CC's read (5.3.5.2.1), not yet his word. Split from b38af5fd1852 by the orchestrator under RULE 1.
traces_to: CP1 and Law 7 (a deliberate quiet exit is a designed shape, a failed --force is loud); outline 5.3.5.2.
how: In bus/server.py serve, when claim() returns None: exit 0 silently unless --force; with --force find the holder's pid (decide the mechanism: a pid written under the lock), kill it, retry claim() until the kernel frees it, else exit 3 loudly. Add --force to bus/__main__.py argparse. New proof against a scratch CAIRN_BUS_HOME, never the live bus, one tooth per clause.
